transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-02-03
Start time (PST): 15:00
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE); Ethan Liu (Redwood SE); Samir Khan (Cobalt - Head of Platform); Lena Ortiz (Cobalt - ML Eng); Markus Vogel (Cobalt - CTO)
Shared links: deck: https://redwood.app/decks/hosted-chat-sandbox, sandbox access (provisioned after call)

---- Auto Summary / Topics (auto-gen, may be incomplete) ----
- Quick intro to hosted chat API and console walkthrough
- Live discussion on streaming behavior, small code sample for curl/SDK
- Retry/backoff patterns and how Redwood falls back to cheaper model variant
- Console Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization and cost tradeoffs

---- Transcript ----
[00:00:05] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account, and Ethan our SE will take the demo pieces. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:12] Samir: Good thanks, Maya. Quick heads up, Markus might need to step out around 15 minutes in.
[00:00:18] Maya: Totally fine. Quick agenda: run through hosted chat basics, show streaming and param controls, then retries and console tips, and end with next steps.
[00:00:27] Lena: Sounds great. We're most interested in latency and predictable cost.
[00:00:31] Ethan: Perfect. I'll start with a quick code snippet, then flip to the console. So generation basics: you call /v1/chat or the conversation endpoint, send in history plus the user message. Streaming is enabled by default with the SDKs.
[00:00:50] [00:00:50] Ethan: So here's a curl example, pardon transcription: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -H "Authorization: Bearer <KEY>" -d '{"messages": [{"role":"user","content":"Where is my shipment?"}], "max_tokens":256, "temperature":0.2}'
[00:01:05] Maya: Note, we also have server SDKs that do chunked streaming so you don't need to poll.
[00:01:12] Samir: When you say streaming is default, does that mean we can start rendering tokens on the client immediately?
[00:01:18] Ethan: Yes, you get partial tokens as they're generated. For websocket or SSE streaming you receive delta tokens. One caution: you have to handle reconnections and idempotency on your side if the client disconnects mid-stream.
[00:01:33] Lena: What about the KV cache you mentioned earlier? We have heavy multi-turn dialogue and want to avoid recomputing context.
[00:01:40] Ethan: Right, our runtime supports KV cache so the prefix is cached on the GPU, which speeds up subsequent tokens. In verbose it's sometimes transcribed as 'K V cache' or 'key V cache' in logs.
[00:01:51] Markus: How do you surface cache hits in the console?
[00:01:54] Ethan: The Console shows token breakdowns and cache hit rates per route — under the Optimize tab we show cost per token and amount saved from cache/batching.
[00:02:05] [00:02:05] Samir: Our SLO is 150ms p50 for short queries (<=64 tokens). Do you commonly hit that on hosted?
[00:02:12] Ethan: With the right model variant and seq length, yes — but there's tradeoffs. For p50 150ms you'd likely pick a lower-precision quantized variant and lower seq length. We can accelerate with dedicated capacity but hosted can hit that for many workloads.
[00:02:28] Lena: Are there automatic fallbacks if load increases? We don't want a hard outage.
[00:02:33] Maya: Yes — smart routing can fall back to compatible model variants or a cheaper tier. For critical paths you can configure automatic fallback policies in the console: e.g., if latency > 400ms for 2 minutes, route to variant B.
[00:02:46] [00:02:46] Samir: And how does retry logic behave during streaming? If the model fails mid-stream, do we re-run the whole request?
[00:02:53] Ethan: Good question. For streaming we recommend client-side retry patterns that are idempotent — e.g., use request IDs and partial token cache. Server-side we attempt transient retries, but for deterministic behavior we usually recommend the client to re-request with the same conversation state; Redwood can accept a resume token in some SDKs but that depends on the SDK version.
[00:03:12] Lena: Resume token — is that part of the public SDK?
[00:03:15] Ethan: It's in the node and python SDKs behind a feature flag in some older transcriptions it was called 'resume token' or 'cursor'. We'll include it in the sandbox build.
[00:03:25] [00:03:25] Markus: Security: can you confirm data at rest encryption and KMS integration?
[00:03:29] Maya: Yes, hosted supports customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated. For hosted we offer encryption at rest and we can discuss dedicated KMS options for enterprise tiers. We'll attach our SOC2 + encryption docs after call.
[00:03:42] Samir: Great. Also, we need data residency in EU for some routes — is that supported?
[00:03:47] Maya: We have region routing; you can pin routes to regions and we can provision EU-based model hosts. For fully on-prem or V P C control, Redwood Private is the path.
[00:03:58] Lena: Back to params — can you talk about temperature and top_p impacts on latency and token usage?
[00:04:03] Ethan: Sure. Temperature/top_p primarily affect sampling behavior and output variance; they don't materially change per-token compute time, but less deterministic outputs might be longer, which increases tokens consumed. max_tokens of course caps it. If you want predictable costs, enforce stop sequences and max_tokens, and consider nucleus sampling with low top_p.
[00:04:23] [00:04:23] Samir: Any tips to reduce tokens without hurting user experience?
[00:04:27] Ethan: Prompt engineering: compress system messages, use token compressing methods, and prefix/key-value cache. Also use embeddings rerankers when you have search + generation combos — that's often more cost-effective.
[00:04:39] Lena: About retries — what's the recommended exponential backoff and jitter?
[00:04:44] Ethan: We usually recommend a small immediate retry for 500-level transient errors with idempotency token, then exponential backoff starting at 200ms with randomized jitter up to 50%. For higher loads, prefer queueing on client and let backend scale.
[00:04:58] [00:04:58] Samir: If a model times out on a single token, does Redwood return partial result or an error?
[00:05:04] Ethan: If it's a hard timeout you'll get an error; if it's an interrupt we may stream partial tokens and append an error event. Client should be prepared to surface a truncated result.
[00:05:14] Markus: Could you demo a live generate in the sandbox?
[00:05:17] Ethan: Sure, I'm switching to the sandbox. Give me 10 seconds.
[00:05:25] [00:05:25] Ethan: Alright, I have a sandbox key. I'm firing a 1-turn query, watch the streaming tokens come in — you'll see the console log a token stream and the token-per-millisecond graph.
[00:05:37] Maya: (whisper) the visualizer sometimes gets labelled as 'token per ms' in older consoles — ignore that if you see odd labels.
[00:05:43] [00:05:43] Lena: I see partial chunks. Does the console let us replay a failed stream?
[00:05:47] Ethan: You can re-run a request via the history and replay it; for production we recommend instrumenting with request_id and logs.
[00:05:54] [00:05:54] Samir: If we want guaranteed exactly-once for billing, what's the pattern?
[00:05:59] Ethan: Use idempotency tokens and server-side dedupe. Billing is per token emitted; if you re-run and it emits tokens again, it'll count. So careful with retries for billing-sensitive flows.
[00:06:12] [00:06:12] Markus: Console Optimize — can it suggest batching levels automatically?
[00:06:16] Ethan: Yes, Optimize analyzes your route patterns and suggests batching profiles and quantization that balance latency and cost. We'll show a sample recommendation in the Optimize tab — e.g., batch up to 16 requests or reduce precision to 4-bit for specific models.
[00:06:30] Lena: Quantization suggestions — are those safe for generation quality? We can't degrade customer UX.
[00:06:35] Ethan: Optimize gives a predicted quality delta and you can run A/B tests from the Console — it ties back to eval results. For sensitive paths, keep higher precision.
[00:06:46] [00:06:46] Samir: Do you have prebuilt metrics or do we integrate with Prometheus?
[00:06:51] Maya: Both. The Console has first-class metrics and you can export traces/metrics to Prometheus/Datadog. Integrations list in the repo.
[00:06:59] Markus: Ok can you summarize the retry and streaming recommended pattern for our engineers?
[00:07:04] Ethan: Sure: 1) Use streaming SDKs and render delta tokens as they arrive; 2) Add request-id/idempotency token; 3) For transient 5xx errors, do a limited immediate retry plus exponential backoff with jitter; 4) For streaming interruptions, re-request with conversation state and resume token where available; 5) Monitor token billing and use max_tokens/stop sequences to cap outputs.
[00:07:29] [00:07:29] Lena: That helps. One more — latency under load: how can we simulate?
[00:07:34] Ethan: We'll provide a small perf harness in the sandbox to run concurrent sessions. We'll also share a benchmark sheet with p50/p95 numbers across model variants.
[00:07:43] Maya: I'll attach the benchmark sheet after the call.
[00:07:46] [00:07:46] Samir: Any known gotchas?
[00:07:49] Ethan: Watch for client-side idle timeouts — some clients close connections after X seconds and that can look like server failures. Also pay attention to tokenization differences across models — some models tokenize more aggressively.
[00:08:02] [00:08:02] Markus: Can you do a short demo of a fallback policy in the console?
[00:08:06] Ethan: Yep — opening the console. Under Routes -> Policies we can set fallback to 'variant-b' if latency exceeds threshold. I'll create a policy: if rolling p95 > 400ms for 2m, then route to 'gpt-small-quant' or similar variant.
[00:08:22] [00:08:22] Ethan: Note, names in my console are example only; in transcription it may read 'g p t small quant' — product names sometimes get munged.
[00:08:30] Lena: For data residency, can we link route to EU region?
[00:08:33] Maya: Yes, you can attach a region tag to route or pin to EU cluster. We'll include exact steps in the doc.
[00:08:38] [00:08:38] Samir: We're keen to run a two-week pilot limited to 100k tokens/day to validate latency. Will that be enough for you to get meaningful metrics?
[00:08:46] Ethan: Absolutely — the sandbox perf harness plus your prompt set will give us p50/p95 curves. For billing we'll simulate conservative token counts.
[00:08:56] [00:08:56] Maya: Any questions on pricing tiers? We have hosted usage-based and dedicated if you want guaranteed throughput.
[00:09:02] Markus: For now hosted is fine, but we may move to dedicated if throughput becomes critical.
[00:09:06] [00:09:06] Lena: Ok, last technical: does Redwood support function calling / structured outputs?
[00:09:11] Ethan: Yes, we support function/tool calling semantics and structured JSON outputs. Console can validate outputs against a schema.
[00:09:20] [00:09:20] Samir: Great, thanks.
[00:09:22] Ethan: Quick wrap: I'll provision sandbox and run the perf test, Maya will send SOC2 and security notes, Lena will share prompts and latency targets.
[00:09:32] Maya: I'll create a follow-up calendar invite for the 48-hour check-in.
[00:09:36] Lena: Sounds good.
[00:09:39] [00:09:39] (crosstalk) Markus: Thanks all — good demo.
[00:09:42] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
